question: How do I make a new claim for Universal Credit?
answer: You can make a new claim for Universal Credit online by creating an account and completing your claim within 28 days of creating the account [1]. Your claim starts on the date you submit it in your account [1]. If you live with your partner, you both need to create accounts and link them together when you claim [1]. If you cannot claim online, you can claim by phone through the Universal Credit helpline [1].

question: Can I get Universal Credit if I am employed but on a low income?
answer: Yes, you can get Universal Credit if you are employed but on a low income [1]. There is no limit to how many hours you can work and still get Universal Credit [4]. Your Universal Credit payment will reduce as you earn more, but for every £1 you earn, your payment only goes down by 55p [4]. If you or your partner are responsible for a child or have a disability or health condition that affects your ability to work, you may be able to earn a certain amount before your payment starts to reduce — this is called a 'work allowance' [6].

question: What is Employment and Support Allowance?
answer:
Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) is a benefit for people who have a disability or health condition that affects how much they can work [1]. It provides money to help with living costs if you’re unable to work and offers support to get back into work if you’re able to [1]. 

New Style ESA is a fortnightly payment that can be claimed on its own or at the same time as Universal Credit [4]. If you receive both, your Universal Credit payment is reduced by the amount you get for New Style ESA [4]. New Style ESA is a contributory benefit, meaning you may be eligible if you’ve paid or been credited with enough National Insurance contributions in the 2 full tax years before the year you’re claiming in [4].

question: What is Statutory Shared Parental Leave?
answer: Statutory Shared Parental Leave (SPL) is leave that may be available if an employee or their partner ends maternity or adoption leave or pay early, making the remaining leave available as SPL [3]. SPL and Statutory Shared Parental Pay (ShPP) must be taken between the baby’s birth and first birthday, or within 1 year of adoption [3]. The employee must also give the correct notice, including a declaration that their partner meets the employment and income requirements [2].

question: What is unfair dismissal and how do I claim it?
answer: Unfair dismissal occurs when your employer does not have a good reason for dismissing you or does not follow the correct process, such as the company’s formal disciplinary or dismissal procedure [1]. A dismissal may be automatically unfair if it is related to reasons such as pregnancy, family leave, whistleblowing, joining a trade union, or taking part in lawful industrial action [3]. You may be able to claim unfair dismissal if you are an employee and have worked for your employer for the qualifying period. Normally, this is 2 years in Great Britain and 1 year in Northern Ireland [2]. There is no qualifying period if you have been dismissed because of your political opinions or affiliation since 25 June 2013 [2]. To claim, you can go to an employment tribunal if you cannot resolve the issue with your employer [2]. In Northern Ireland, you go to an industrial tribunal [2].

This amount must be rounded up to the nearest hour if the entitlement is 0.5 of an hour or more [3]. The worker’s ‘normal’ rate of pay must be used for all leave, which includes commission, regular overtime payments, and payments related to length of service or professional qualifications, but not usually bonus payments [1].

question: How large is the Right to Buy discount?
answer:
The Right to Buy discount is the lower of:

- 70% of the value of your property, or  
- the maximum discount for your region [2].

The maximum regional discounts are:

- North East: £22,000  
- North West: £26,000  
- Yorkshire and the Humber: £24,000  
- East Midlands: £24,000  
- West Midlands: £26,000  
- Eastern: £34,000 (but £16,000 in Watford)  
- South East: £38,000 (but £16,000 in certain areas)  
- South West: £30,000  
- London: £16,000 (but £38,000 in Barking and Dagenham and Havering) [2].

If you applied to buy your home before 21 November 2024, the maximum discount is the lower of:

- 70% of the value of your property  
- £136,400 if your home is in a London borough  
- £102,400 if your home is outside London [2].

The guidance does not state the exact discount for every individual case, as it depends on property value and location.

question: How do I apply for council housing?
answer: You apply for council housing through your local council [1]. question: What repairs is a landlord responsible for?
answer:
A landlord is always responsible for repairs to the property’s structure and exterior, fire safety issues, basins, sinks, baths and other sanitary fittings including pipes and drains, heating and hot water, gas appliances, pipes, flues and ventilation, and electrical wiring [1]. The landlord is also responsible for any damage they cause by attempting repairs [1]. In blocks of flats, the landlord is usually responsible for repairing common areas, such as staircases [1].

In shared ownership homes during the initial repair period, the landlord is responsible for the cost of essential repairs to the outside of the building and essential structural repairs to walls, floors, ceiling and stairs inside the home [2]. The landlord may also contribute up to £500 a year towards repairing, replacing (if faulty) and maintaining fixtures and fittings that supply water, gas or electricity or heat the home [2].

If a landlord does not carry out repairs, the tenant can contact the environmental health department at their local council, which must take action if the problems could harm the tenant or cause a nuisance to others [1]. In Scotland, the tenant should contact the Private Rented Housing Panel (PRHP) [1]. If serious hazards are found under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS), the council must take enforcement action to remove the hazard [4].

question: What is a House in Multiple Occupation (HMO)?
answer: A House in Multiple Occupation (HMO) is a property rented out to at least 3 people who are from more than one household and who share toilet, bathroom, or kitchen facilities [2]. A household is either a single person or members of the same family living together, including people who are married, living together (including same-sex relationships), relatives, half-relatives, or step-parents and step-children [2]. This definition applies in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, though licensing processes differ by region [3][4]. In Northern Ireland, an HMO is also known as a 'house share' [3].

question: What is the Right to Acquire for housing association tenants?
answer:
The Right to Acquire is a scheme that allows housing association tenants to buy their rented home at a discount, provided they and their landlord meet certain eligibility requirements [1]. To qualify, tenants must have had a public sector landlord, such as a housing association, council, armed services, or NHS trust, for at least 3 years [1]. The property must be self-contained, the tenant’s main home, and either built or bought by a housing association after 31 March 1997 with social housing grant funding, or transferred from a council to a housing association after that date [1]. The landlord must also be registered with the Regulator of Social Housing [1].

Eligible tenants can receive a discount between £9,000 and £16,000, depending on where they live in the UK, though this may be reduced if they have previously used Right to Acquire or Right to Buy [3]. Tenants can apply using a Right to Acquire application form sent to their landlord, who must respond within 4 weeks (or 8 weeks if they have been the landlord for less than 3 years) [2]. If the landlord agrees to sell, they must make an offer within 8 weeks for a freehold or 12 weeks for a leasehold property [2].

The offer will include the proposed price, discount, property description, estimated service charges for flats or maisonettes, and any known structural issues [5]. Tenants have 12 weeks to accept the offer, with reminders (RTA4 and RTA5) sent if no response is given, after which the application may be dropped [5]. Tenants can withdraw from the sale at any time and continue renting [5].

question: What are my rights as a leaseholder regarding service charges?
answer:
As a leaseholder, your rights regarding service charges include:

- You have the right to be consulted about charges for running or maintaining the building if you have to pay more than £250 for planned work or £100 per year for work and services lasting more than 12 months. This is known as a ‘Section 20’ consultation [1].

- You have the right to get information about service charges [3].

- You may be able to apply to a tribunal if you think a charge is unreasonable, if the standard of work is unsatisfactory, or if you do not think you should be paying it at all [1]. However, you cannot apply to the tribunal if you’ve agreed to pay the charge, the dispute is already being dealt with by a court, or you pay a fixed charge [1].

- You have the right to challenge certain charges under some circumstances [3].

- Service charges must not be higher than the actual cost of delivering the services, as required by the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 [2].

The guidance does not specify your right to receive a detailed breakdown of service charge costs beyond the right to information and consultation.
